questions.subject: Physics
questions.questionText: An inclined plane is inclined at an angle $\beta = 30^\circ$ to the horizontal. A particle is projected from the foot of the incline with an initial speed $u = 20\text{ m/s}$ at an angle $\alpha = 30^\circ$ with respect to the inclined surface. Taking $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$, find the time of flight $T$ of the projectile along the inclined plane.
questions.explanation: Choose coordinate axes parallel and perpendicular to the inclined plane: the $x$-axis lies along the incline pointing upwards and the $y$-axis is normal to the incline. The initial velocity components are $u_x = u\cos\alpha = 20\cos 30^\circ = 10\sqrt{3}\text{ m/s}$ and $u_y = u\sin\alpha = 20\sin 30^\circ = 10\text{ m/s}$. The acceleration components due to gravity are $a_x = -g\sin\beta = -10\sin 30^\circ = -5\text{ m/s}^2$ and $a_y = -g\cos\beta = -10\cos 30^\circ = -5\sqrt{3}\text{ m/s}^2$. Setting displacement perpendicular to the incline $y(T) = u_y T + \frac{1}{2}a_y T^2 = 0$, we get $T = \frac{2u_y}{|a_y|} = \frac{2(10)}{5\sqrt{3}} = \frac{4}{\sqrt{3}}\text{ s}$. Therefore, option A is correct. Option B misses the factor of $2$, yielding $\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\text{ s}$. Option C uses standard horizontal ground formula $\frac{2u\sin 60^\circ}{g} = 2\sqrt{3}\text{ s}$. Option D uses $g\sin\beta$ instead of $g\cos\beta$ in the denominator.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.questionText: A projectile is launched from the foot of an inclined plane of inclination angle $\beta = 30^\circ$ with an initial launch speed $u$. If the projectile strikes the inclined plane perpendicularly at the end of its flight, determine the value of $\tan\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle of projection with respect to the horizontal.
questions.explanation: Let the projectile launch angle with the incline be $\alpha = \theta - \beta$. The components of initial velocity are $u_x = u\cos\alpha$ along the incline and $u_y = u\sin\alpha$ perpendicular to the incline. The acceleration components are $a_x = -g\sin\beta$ and $a_y = -g\cos\beta$. The time of flight is $T = \frac{2u_y}{|a_y|} = \frac{2u\sin\alpha}{g\cos\beta}$. For the projectile to strike the incline perpendicularly, the velocity component along the incline must vanish at time $T$, so $v_x(T) = u\cos\alpha - g\sin\beta T = 0$. Substituting $T$, we get $u\cos\alpha = g\sin\beta \left(\frac{2u\sin\alpha}{g\cos\beta}\right) = 2u\tan\beta\sin\alpha$. Therefore, $\cot\alpha = 2\tan\beta$. Since $\beta = 30^\circ$, $\tan\beta = 1/\sqrt{3}$, yielding $\cot\alpha = 2/\sqrt{3} \implies \tan\alpha = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$. Now applying the tangent addition formula: $\tan\theta = \tan(\alpha + \beta) = \frac{\tan\alpha + \tan\beta}{1 - \tan\alpha\tan\beta} = \frac{\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}}{1 - \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}} = \frac{\frac{5}{2\sqrt{3}}}{\frac{1}{2}} = \frac{5}{\sqrt{3}}$. Hence, option A is correct.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.questionText: A river of width $w = 300\text{ m}$ flows at a constant speed of $u = 5\text{ m/s}$. A swimmer can swim with a speed $v = 3\text{ m/s}$ in still water. If the swimmer steers at an angle such that the downstream drift along the opposite bank is minimized, find the minimum drift in metres.
questions.explanation: Since the swimmer speed $v = 3\text{ m/s}$ is less than the river current $u = 5\text{ m/s}$, zero drift cannot be achieved. Let the swimmer head at an angle $\phi$ with respect to the upstream direction. The components of velocity relative to the ground are $v_x = u - v\cos\phi$ and $v_y = v\sin\phi$. The time to cross is $t = \frac{w}{v\sin\phi}$. The downstream drift is $x = v_x t = \frac{w(u - v\cos\phi)}{v\sin\phi} = w\left(\frac{u}{v}\csc\phi - \cot\phi\right)$. To minimize drift with respect to $\phi$, differentiating yields $\frac{dx}{d\phi} = w\left(-\frac{u}{v}\csc\phi\cot\phi + \csc^2\phi\right) = 0$, implying $\cos\phi = \frac{v}{u} = \frac{3}{5}$. Consequently, $\sin\phi = \frac{4}{5}$. Substituting these values into the drift expression, we get $x_{\min} = 300\left(\frac{5}{3}\cdot\frac{5}{4} - \frac{3}{4}\right) = 300\left(\frac{25-9}{12}\right) = 300\left(\frac{16}{12}\right) = 400\text{ m}$. Hence, the minimum drift is $400$ metres.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.questionText: A motorboat can travel with speed $v = 5\text{ m/s}$ in still water. A straight river of width $d = 240\text{ m}$ flows at a uniform speed of $u = 3\text{ m/s}$. In Case 1, the boat steers directly perpendicular to the river bank to cross in the minimum possible time $t_1$. In Case 2, the boat heads upstream at an angle such that it reaches the opposite bank directly across from the starting point without any drift, taking time $t_2$. Calculate the ratio $\frac{t_2}{t_1}$.
questions.explanation: In Case 1, to minimize crossing time, the boat must direct its velocity purely perpendicular to the flow, so $v_y = v = 5\text{ m/s}$. The minimum crossing time is $t_1 = \frac{d}{v} = \frac{240}{5} = 48\text{ s}$. In Case 2, for zero drift, the boat must aim upstream at an angle $\theta$ such that $v\sin\theta = u = 3\text{ m/s}$. The effective velocity across the river is $v_{\text{eff}} = \sqrt{v^2 - u^2} = \sqrt{5^2 - 3^2} = 4\text{ m/s}$. Thus, the crossing time is $t_2 = \frac{d}{\sqrt{v^2 - u^2}} = \frac{240}{4} = 60\text{ s}$. The ratio of the times is $\frac{t_2}{t_1} = \frac{60}{48} = \frac{5}{4}$. Therefore, option A is correct. Option B inverts the ratio. Option C uses $v/u = 5/3$. Option D uses $\sqrt{v^2-u^2}/u = 4/3$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.questionText: A person walking along a horizontal road at a speed of $3\text{ km/h}$ observes rain drops falling vertically downward. When the person doubles their speed to $6\text{ km/h}$ in the same direction, the rain drops appear to strike the person at an angle of $45^\circ$ with the vertical. Determine the actual speed of the rain drops with respect to the ground.
questions.explanation: Let the true velocity of rain relative to the ground be $\vec{v}_r = v_{rx}\hat{i} + v_{ry}\hat{j}$. In the first case, the person velocity is $\vec{v}_{m1} = 3\hat{i}\text{ km/h}$. The relative velocity is $\vec{v}_{r/m1} = (v_{rx} - 3)\hat{i} + v_{ry}\hat{j}$. Since the rain appears vertical, the horizontal component is zero: $v_{rx} - 3 = 0 \implies v_{rx} = 3\text{ km/h}$. In the second case, $\vec{v}_{m2} = 6\hat{i}\text{ km/h}$, so $\vec{v}_{r/m2} = (3 - 6)\hat{i} + v_{ry}\hat{j} = -3\hat{i} + v_{ry}\hat{j}$. The angle with the vertical is $45^\circ$, implying $\tan 45^\circ = \frac{|v_{r/m2,x}|}{|v_{r/m2,y}|} = \frac{3}{|v_{ry}|} = 1$, yielding $|v_{ry}| = 3\text{ km/h}$. Since the rain falls downward, $v_{ry} = -3\text{ km/h}$. The true speed of the rain relative to the ground is $v_r = \sqrt{v_{rx}^2 + v_{ry}^2} = \sqrt{3^2 + (-3)^2} = 3\sqrt{2}\text{ km/h}$. Therefore, option A is correct.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.questionText: Rain is falling vertically downward with a speed of $v_r = 20\text{ m/s}$ relative to the ground. A cyclist rides down a straight slope inclined at an angle $\theta = 37^\circ$ to the horizontal (with $\sin 37^\circ = 3/5$, $\cos 37^\circ = 4/5$). At what speed $v_c$ (in m/s) must the cyclist ride down the slope so that the rain appears to strike the cyclist perpendicularly to the inclined plane?
questions.explanation: Define the coordinate system where $\hat{i}$ is horizontal along the direction of descent and $\hat{j}$ is vertically upward. The velocity of rain is $\vec{v}_r = -20\hat{j}\text{ m/s}$. The unit vector along the inclined plane downwards is $\hat{u}_{\parallel} = \cos 37^\circ\hat{i} - \sin 37^\circ\hat{j} = \frac{4}{5}\hat{i} - \frac{3}{5}\hat{j}$. The cyclist velocity moving down the incline is $\vec{v}_c = v_c\hat{u}_{\parallel} = v_c\left(\frac{4}{5}\hat{i} - \frac{3}{5}\hat{j}\right)$. The relative velocity of rain with respect to the cyclist is $\vec{v}_{r/c} = \vec{v}_r - \vec{v}_c = -\frac{4}{5}v_c\hat{i} + \left(-20 + \frac{3}{5}v_c\right)\hat{j}$. For the rain to strike perpendicularly to the incline, the component of $\vec{v}_{r/c}$ along the incline must vanish, meaning $\vec{v}_{r/c} \cdot \hat{u}_{\parallel} = 0$. Substituting the components: $\left(-\frac{4}{5}v_c\right)\left(\frac{4}{5}\right) + \left(-20 + \frac{3}{5}v_c\right)\left(-\frac{3}{5}\right) = 0 \implies -\frac{16}{25}v_c + 12 - \frac{9}{25}v_c = 0$. This simplifies to $-v_c + 12 = 0 \implies v_c = 12\text{ m/s}$. Hence, the required speed is $12$ m/s.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.questionText: A particle launched from level ground with speed $u$ at an angle $\theta$ above the horizontal passes through two points at the same height $h = 15\text{ m}$ at instants $t_1 = 1\text{ s}$ and $t_2 = 3\text{ s}$. Taking $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$, find the maximum height $H_{\max}$ reached by the projectile above the ground.
questions.explanation: The vertical position of the projectile at time $t$ is given by $y(t) = u_y t - \frac{1}{2}gt^2$. Setting $y(t) = h$ yields the quadratic equation $\frac{1}{2}gt^2 - u_y t + h = 0$, or $5t^2 - u_y t + 15 = 0$. The roots of this equation are $t_1$ and $t_2$. By Vieta relations, the sum of the roots is $t_1 + t_2 = \frac{u_y}{5}$. Substituting $t_1 = 1\text{ s}$ and $t_2 = 3\text{ s}$, we get $1 + 3 = 4 = \frac{u_y}{5} \implies u_y = 20\text{ m/s}$. Checking the product: $t_1 t_2 = 15/5 = 3$, which matches $1 \times 3 = 3$. The maximum height reached by the projectile is given by $H_{\max} = \frac{u_y^2}{2g} = \frac{20^2}{2(10)} = \frac{400}{20} = 20\text{ m}$. Therefore, option A is correct. Option B mistakenly computes $h + \frac{1}{2}g((t_2-t_1)/2)^2 = 15 + 5 = 20$ with an arithmetic error of $15 + 10 = 25\text{ m}$. Option C doubles the given height. Option D incorrectly applies a $\sqrt{2}$ factor.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.questionText: Two particles $A$ and $B$ are projected simultaneously from the origin in the same vertical plane. Particle $A$ is projected with speed $u_A = 20\text{ m/s}$ at an angle of $60^\circ$ to the horizontal, and particle $B$ is projected with speed $u_B = 20\sqrt{3}\text{ m/s}$ at an angle of $30^\circ$ to the horizontal. Taking $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$, find the separation between the particles at $t = 2\text{ s}$ while both are still in flight.
questions.explanation: Since both particles move under the influence of uniform gravity $\vec{g} = -10\hat{j}\text{ m/s}^2$, their relative acceleration is $\vec{a}_{\text{rel}} = \vec{g} - \vec{g} = \vec{0}$. Consequently, the relative velocity $\vec{v}_{A/B} = \vec{u}_A - \vec{u}_B$ remains strictly constant throughout the flight. Calculating the initial velocity components: $\vec{u}_A = (20\cos 60^\circ)\hat{i} + (20\sin 60^\circ)\hat{j} = 10\hat{i} + 10\sqrt{3}\hat{j}\text{ m/s}$, and $\vec{u}_B = (20\sqrt{3}\cos 30^\circ)\hat{i} + (20\sqrt{3}\sin 30^\circ)\hat{j} = 30\hat{i} + 10\sqrt{3}\hat{j}\text{ m/s}$. The relative velocity is $\vec{v}_{A/B} = (10 - 30)\hat{i} + (10\sqrt{3} - 10\sqrt{3})\hat{j} = -20\hat{i}\text{ m/s}$. Both particles have total flight time $T = \frac{2u_y}{g} = \frac{2(10\sqrt{3})}{10} = 2\sqrt{3} \approx 3.46\text{ s} > 2\text{ s}$, so both are in flight at $t = 2\text{ s}$. The separation between the particles at $t = 2\text{ s}$ is $|\Delta\vec{r}| = |\vec{v}_{A/B}| \cdot t = 20 \times 2 = 40\text{ m}$. Therefore, option A is correct.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.questionText: A ball is projected horizontally with an initial speed $u = 15\text{ m/s}$ from the top of an inclined plane of inclination angle $\theta = 45^\circ$ with the horizontal. Taking $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$, find the total distance along the inclined plane from the launch point to the point of impact.
questions.explanation: Set the launch point at the origin $(0,0)$. The equation of the inclined surface sloping downward to the right is $y = -x\tan 45^\circ = -x$. The equations of motion of the ball are $x(t) = ut = 15t$ and $y(t) = -\frac{1}{2}gt^2 = -5t^2$. At the point of impact on the incline, $y(t) = -x(t)$, which yields $-5t^2 = -15t$. For $t > 0$, solving gives $t = 3\text{ s}$. The horizontal displacement is $x = 15 \times 3 = 45\text{ m}$ and the vertical displacement is $y = -45\text{ m}$. The distance along the incline is $s = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} = \sqrt{45^2 + (-45)^2} = 45\sqrt{2}\text{ m}$. Therefore, option A is correct. Option B comes from an incorrect time of flight $t = 2\text{ s}$. Option C reports only the horizontal coordinate $x$. Option D doubles the coordinate.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.questionText: A projectile is launched from ground level to clear a vertical wall of height $h = 15\text{ m}$ located at a horizontal distance $d = 20\text{ m}$ from the launch position. Taking $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$, find the minimum launch speed $u_{\min}$ (in m/s) required to clear the wall.
questions.explanation: The trajectory equation is $y = x\tan\theta - \frac{g x^2}{2u^2}(1 + \tan^2\theta)$. For the projectile to pass through the point $(d, h) = (20, 15)$, we substitute the values: $15 = 20\tan\theta - \frac{10(20)^2}{2u^2}(1 + \tan^2\theta) = 20\tan\theta - \frac{2000}{u^2}(1 + \tan^2\theta)$. Rearranging as a quadratic in $\tan\theta$: $\frac{2000}{u^2}\tan^2\theta - 20\tan\theta + \left(15 + \frac{2000}{u^2}\right) = 0$. For a real trajectory to exist, the discriminant must be non-negative: $\Delta = (-20)^2 - 4\left(\frac{2000}{u^2}\right)\left(15 + \frac{2000}{u^2}\right) \geq 0$. This gives $400 - \frac{8000}{u^2}\left(15 + \frac{2000}{u^2}\right) \geq 0 \implies 1 - \frac{20}{u^2}\left(15 + \frac{2000}{u^2}\right) \geq 0$. Multiplying by $u^4$: $u^4 - 300 u^2 - 40000 \geq 0$. Factoring the quadratic in $u^2$: $(u^2 - 400)(u^2 + 100) \geq 0$. Since $u^2 > 0$, we get $u^2 \geq 400 \implies u_{\min} = 20\text{ m/s}$. Hence, the minimum launch speed is $20$ m/s.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.questionText: A high-speed motorboat moves along a straight line with an initial speed $v_0 = 10\text{ m/s}$. After the engine is shut off at $t = 0$, the water resistance creates a deceleration given by $a = -k v^2$, where $k = 0.1\text{ m}^{-1}$ and $v$ is the instantaneous speed. Find the distance travelled by the boat by the time its speed reduces to $v = 2\text{ m/s}$.
questions.explanation: Expressing acceleration in terms of position: $a = v\frac{dv}{dx} = -k v^2$. Dividing both sides by $v$, we get $\frac{dv}{v} = -k\,dx$. Integrating both sides from the initial state $(x=0, v=v_0)$ to the final state $(x, v)$: $\int_{v_0}^v \frac{dv}{v} = -k\int_0^x dx \implies \ln\left(\frac{v}{v_0}\right) = -kx$. Solving for the displacement $x$: $x = \frac{1}{k}\ln\left(\frac{v_0}{v}\right)$. Substituting the given values $k = 0.1 = \frac{1}{10}\text{ m}^{-1}$, $v_0 = 10\text{ m/s}$, and $v = 2\text{ m/s}$: $x = 10\ln\left(\frac{10}{2}\right) = 10\ln 5\text{ m}$. Therefore, option A is correct. Option B incorrectly replaces $1/k$ with $v_0/2 = 5$. Option C uses $v$ instead of $v_0/v$. Option D erroneously applies uniform deceleration equations.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.questionText: A particle moves along the positive $x$-axis subject to a position-dependent acceleration $a(x) = 2x + 5$ (in m/s$^2$), where $x$ is in metres. If the particle passes through the origin $x = 0$ with a speed of $v = 4\text{ m/s}$, find its speed (in m/s) when it reaches $x = 3\text{ m}$.
questions.explanation: Using the kinematic relation $a = v\frac{dv}{dx}$, we can write $v\,dv = a(x)\,dx = (2x + 5)\,dx$. Integrating both sides from $x = 0$ (where $v = 4\text{ m/s}$) to $x = 3\text{ m}$ (where velocity is $v$): $\int_4^v v'\,dv' = \int_0^3 (2x + 5)\,dx$. Evaluating the integrals: $\left[\frac{v'^2}{2}\right]_4^v = \left[x^2 + 5x\right]_0^3 \implies \frac{v^2 - 16}{2} = 3^2 + 5(3) = 9 + 15 = 24$. Multiplying by $2$ gives $v^2 - 16 = 48 \implies v^2 = 64$. Taking the positive square root for speed yields $v = 8\text{ m/s}$. Hence, the particle speed at $x = 3\text{ m}$ is $8$ m/s.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.questionText: A particle moves along a straight line such that its velocity varies linearly with displacement $x$ according to $v(x) = v_0 \left(1 - \frac{x}{L}\right)$ for $0 \leq x \leq L$, where $v_0 = 20\text{ m/s}$ and $L = 50\text{ m}$. Determine the magnitude of the acceleration of the particle at displacement $x = 20\text{ m}$.
questions.explanation: The acceleration is related to velocity and position by $a = v\frac{dv}{dx}$. Differentiating the velocity function with respect to $x$: $\frac{dv}{dx} = -\frac{v_0}{L}$. Substituting this into the acceleration expression yields $a(x) = v_0\left(1 - \frac{x}{L}\right)\left(-\frac{v_0}{L}\right) = -\frac{v_0^2}{L}\left(1 - \frac{x}{L}\right)$. Given $v_0 = 20\text{ m/s}$ and $L = 50\text{ m}$, the prefactor is $\frac{v_0^2}{L} = \frac{400}{50} = 8\text{ m/s}^2$. At displacement $x = 20\text{ m}$, the term in parentheses evaluates to $1 - \frac{20}{50} = 1 - 0.4 = 0.6$. Thus, the magnitude of the acceleration is $|a| = 8 \times 0.6 = 4.8\text{ m/s}^2$. Therefore, option A is correct. Option B calculates $8 \times 0.4 = 3.2\text{ m/s}^2$. Option C ignores the factor $(1 - x/L)$. Option D introduces an extraneous factor of $1/2$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.questionText: A particle starts from rest at $t = 0$ and moves along the positive $x$-axis with an acceleration $a = \alpha\sqrt{v}$, where $\alpha = 4\text{ m}^{1/2}/\text{s}^{3/2}$ and $v$ is its instantaneous velocity. Find the distance traversed by the particle in the first $t = 3\text{ s}$ of its motion.
questions.explanation: From the definition of acceleration, $\frac{dv}{dt} = \alpha\sqrt{v} \implies \frac{dv}{\sqrt{v}} = \alpha\,dt$. Integrating both sides from rest ($v=0$ at $t=0$): $\int_0^v v'^{-1/2}\,dv' = \alpha\int_0^t dt' \implies 2\sqrt{v} = \alpha t \implies v(t) = \frac{\alpha^2 t^2}{4}$. Substituting $\alpha = 4\text{ m}^{1/2}/\text{s}^{3/2}$, we obtain $v(t) = \frac{16 t^2}{4} = 4t^2\text{ m/s}$. The distance travelled is obtained by integrating velocity with respect to time: $x(t) = \int_0^t v(t')\,dt' = \int_0^t 4t'^2\,dt' = \frac{4}{3}t^3$. At time $t = 3\text{ s}$, the distance is $x(3) = \frac{4}{3}(3)^3 = \frac{4}{3} \times 27 = 36\text{ m}$. Therefore, option A is correct. Option B erroneously uses $x = \frac{1}{2}at^2$. Option C computes $\frac{\alpha^2 t^3}{2} = 54\text{ m}$. Option D multiplies instantaneous velocity $v(3)$ by total time $t = 3\text{ s}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.questionText: The trajectory of a projectile launched in a vertical plane is described by the equation $y = \sqrt{3}x - \frac{gx^2}{20}$, where $x$ and $y$ are measured in metres and $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$. Find the radius of curvature of the projectile path at its highest point (apex).
questions.explanation: Comparing the given equation $y = \sqrt{3}x - \frac{gx^2}{20}$ with the standard trajectory equation $y = x\tan\theta - \frac{gx^2}{2u^2\cos^2\theta}$, we identify $\tan\theta = \sqrt{3} \implies \theta = 60^\circ$, so $\cos\theta = 1/2$. Matching the coefficient of $x^2$: $2u^2\cos^2\theta = 20 \implies 2u^2\left(\frac{1}{4}\right) = 20 \implies u^2 = 40\text{ m}^2/\text{s}^2$. At the highest point of the trajectory, the vertical velocity is zero and the speed is purely horizontal: $v_{\text{apex}} = u\cos 60^\circ = \sqrt{40}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) = \sqrt{10}\text{ m/s}$. At this point, the acceleration is directed purely perpendicular to the velocity, with magnitude $a_\perp = g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$. Therefore, the radius of curvature is $\rho = \frac{v_{\text{apex}}^2}{a_\perp} = \frac{10}{10} = 1\text{ m}$. Alternatively, applying the calculus formula $\rho = \frac{(1 + (y')^2)^{3/2}}{|y''|}$ with $y' = \sqrt{3} - x$ and $y'' = -1$ at $x = \sqrt{3}$ also gives $\rho = 1\text{ m}$. Therefore, option A is correct.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.questionText: A projectile is launched from ground level with an initial speed $u = 40\text{ m/s}$ at an angle $\theta = 37^\circ$ above the horizontal (with $\cos 37^\circ = 4/5$, $\sin 37^\circ = 3/5$). Taking $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$, find the radius of curvature (in metres) of the projectile trajectory at the instant of launch.
questions.explanation: At the instant of launch, the velocity of the projectile is $v = u = 40\text{ m/s}$, directed at an angle $\theta = 37^\circ$ to the horizontal. The acceleration acting on the projectile is the downward acceleration due to gravity $\vec{g}$. The component of acceleration perpendicular to the instantaneous velocity vector provides the centripetal acceleration: $a_\perp = g\cos\theta = 10\cos 37^\circ = 10\left(\frac{4}{5}\right) = 8\text{ m/s}^2$. The radius of curvature of the trajectory is given by $\rho = \frac{v^2}{a_\perp} = \frac{u^2}{g\cos\theta}$. Substituting the numerical values: $\rho = \frac{40^2}{8} = \frac{1600}{8} = 200\text{ m}$. Hence, the radius of curvature at launch is $200$ metres.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.questionText: A particle is projected from the ground with an initial speed $u = 20\text{ m/s}$ at an elevation angle of $60^\circ$ above the horizontal. Taking $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$, find the time $t$ elapsed when the instantaneous velocity vector becomes perpendicular to the initial velocity vector, and find the speed $v$ at that instant.
questions.explanation: The initial velocity vector is $\vec{u} = u\cos 60^\circ\hat{i} + u\sin 60^\circ\hat{j}$. At time $t$, the velocity vector is $\vec{v}(t) = u\cos 60^\circ\hat{i} + (u\sin 60^\circ - gt)\hat{j}$. The condition for $\vec{v}(t)$ to be perpendicular to $\vec{u}$ is $\vec{u} \cdot \vec{v}(t) = 0$. Expanding the dot product: $u^2\cos^2 60^\circ + u\sin 60^\circ(u\sin 60^\circ - gt) = u^2(\cos^2 60^\circ + \sin^2 60^\circ) - ugt\sin 60^\circ = u^2 - ugt\sin 60^\circ = 0$. Solving for $t$ yields $t = \frac{u}{g\sin 60^\circ} = \frac{20}{10(\sqrt{3}/2)} = \frac{4}{\sqrt{3}}\text{ s}$. Furthermore, because $\vec{u} \perp \vec{v}$, the horizontal component remains unchanged: $v_x = u\cos 60^\circ = v\cos(90^\circ - 60^\circ) = v\sin 60^\circ$, which implies $v = u\cot 60^\circ = \frac{20}{\sqrt{3}}\text{ m/s}$. Therefore, option A is correct.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.questionText: A particle starts from the origin $(0,0)$ at $t = 0$ with an initial velocity $\vec{v}_0 = 4\hat{i}\text{ m/s}$ and experiences a time-dependent acceleration $\vec{a}(t) = 6t\hat{i} + 4\hat{j}\text{ m/s}^2$. Find the coordinates $(x, y)$ of the particle and its speed $v$ at time $t = 2\text{ s}$.
questions.explanation: Integrating the acceleration components with respect to time: For the $x$-direction: $v_x(t) = v_{0x} + \int_0^t 6t'\,dt' = 4 + 3t^2$, and $x(t) = \int_0^t (4 + 3t'^2)\,dt' = 4t + t^3$. For the $y$-direction: $v_y(t) = 0 + \int_0^t 4\,dt' = 4t$, and $y(t) = \int_0^t 4t'\,dt' = 2t^2$. Evaluating at $t = 2\text{ s}$: $x(2) = 4(2) + 2^3 = 8 + 8 = 16\text{ m}$, and $y(2) = 2(2^2) = 8\text{ m}$. The velocity components at $t = 2\text{ s}$ are $v_x(2) = 4 + 3(2^2) = 16\text{ m/s}$ and $v_y(2) = 4(2) = 8\text{ m/s}$. The speed is $v = \sqrt{v_x^2 + v_y^2} = \sqrt{16^2 + 8^2} = \sqrt{256 + 64} = \sqrt{320} = 8\sqrt{5}\text{ m/s}$. Therefore, option A is correct.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.questionText: A particle moving along the positive $x$-axis with an initial speed $u = 8\text{ m/s}$ at $x = 0$ experiences a retarding acceleration given by $a = -\alpha\sqrt{x}$, where $\alpha = 6\text{ m}^{1/2}/\text{s}^2$ and $x$ is in metres. Find the stopping distance $x_s$ (in metres) traversed by the particle before it momentarily comes to rest.
questions.explanation: Applying the differential relation $a = v\frac{dv}{dx} = -\alpha x^{1/2}$, we separate variables to obtain $v\,dv = -\alpha x^{1/2}\,dx$. Integrating both sides from the initial point $(x=0, v=u)$ to the stopping point $(x=x_s, v=0)$: $\int_u^0 v\,dv = -\alpha\int_0^{x_s} x^{1/2}\,dx$. Evaluating both integrals: $-\frac{u^2}{2} = -\alpha\left[\frac{2}{3}x_s^{3/2}\right] \implies \frac{u^2}{2} = \frac{2\alpha}{3}x_s^{3/2}$. Rearranging for $x_s^{3/2}$: $x_s^{3/2} = \frac{3u^2}{4\alpha}$. Substituting the given values $u = 8\text{ m/s}$ and $\alpha = 6\text{ m}^{1/2}/\text{s}^2$: $x_s^{3/2} = \frac{3 \times 64}{4 \times 6} = \frac{192}{24} = 8$. Taking both sides to the power of $2/3$: $x_s = 8^{2/3} = (2^3)^{2/3} = 4\text{ m}$. Hence, the stopping distance is $4$ metres.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.questionText: A projectile is launched from the origin on horizontal ground with an elevation angle $\theta$ above the horizontal. At the instant when the projectile reaches its maximum height, the angle of elevation of the projectile as viewed from the launch origin is $\phi$. Find the relationship between $\tan\phi$ and $\tan\theta$.
questions.explanation: At the highest point of the trajectory, the horizontal coordinate of the projectile is half of the horizontal range: $x = \frac{R}{2} = \frac{u^2\sin 2\theta}{2g} = \frac{u^2\sin\theta\cos\theta}{g}$. The vertical coordinate is the maximum height: $y = H_{\max} = \frac{u^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}$. The angle of elevation $\phi$ as viewed from the origin $(0,0)$ satisfies $\tan\phi = \frac{y}{x} = \frac{H_{\max}}{R/2}$. Substituting the expressions: $\tan\phi = \frac{\frac{u^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}}{\frac{u^2\sin\theta\cos\theta}{g}} = \frac{\sin^2\theta}{2\sin\theta\cos\theta} = \frac{\sin\theta}{2\cos\theta} = \frac{1}{2}\tan\theta$. Therefore, $\tan\phi = \frac{1}{2}\tan\theta$, so option A is correct. Option B incorrectly inverts the factor of $2$. Option C uses the full range $R$ in the denominator instead of $R/2$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.questionText: A particle is launched from ground level with speed $u$ at an angle $\theta$ above horizontal. Neglecting air resistance, consider its motion from the launch instant $t = 0$ until it lands on the ground at time $t = T$. Select the correct statement(s):
options: A) The average velocity vector over the entire flight is $u\cos\theta\hat{i}$.
B) The average acceleration vector over the entire flight is $-g\hat{j}$.
C) The magnitude of the change in velocity between launch and landing is $2u\sin\theta$.
D) The minimum speed during the flight is zero.
questions.explanation: The total horizontal displacement over the flight of duration $T = \frac{2u\sin\theta}{g}$ is $\Delta\vec{r} = R\hat{i} = (u\cos\theta T)\hat{i}$. Thus the average velocity is $\vec{v}_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\Delta\vec{r}}{T} = u\cos\theta\hat{i}$, so statement A is correct. The total change in velocity is $\Delta\vec{v} = \vec{v}(T) - \vec{v}(0) = (u\cos\theta\hat{i} - u\sin\theta\hat{j}) - (u\cos\theta\hat{i} + u\sin\theta\hat{j}) = -2u\sin\theta\hat{j}$. The average acceleration is $\vec{a}_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\Delta\vec{v}}{T} = \frac{-2u\sin\theta\hat{j}}{2u\sin\theta/g} = -g\hat{j}$, so statement B is correct. The magnitude of the change in velocity is $|\Delta\vec{v}| = 2u\sin\theta$, so statement C is correct. The minimum speed occurs at the highest point and equals $u\cos\theta \neq 0$, so statement D is incorrect. Hence, the correct choices are A, B, and C.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.questionText: Three identical particles $A$, $B$, and $C$ are initially placed at the vertices of an equilateral triangle of side length $L = 60\text{ m}$. At $t = 0$, all three particles begin moving simultaneously with a constant speed $v = 10\text{ m/s}$, such that $A$ always heads directly towards $B$, $B$ towards $C$, and $C$ towards $A$. Find the time $T$ required for the particles to converge at the centroid, and the total distance $s$ traversed by each particle.
questions.explanation: By the threefold rotational symmetry of the system, the particles always remain at the vertices of an equilateral triangle of shrinking side length $r(t)$. Consider the separation between particles $A$ and $B$. Particle $A$ moves towards $B$ at speed $v$, while particle $B$ moves towards $C$ at speed $v$ at an angle of $60^\circ$ relative to the line $AB$. The component of velocity of $B$ along the line directed towards $A$ is $-v\cos 60^\circ = -v/2$. The rate of decrease of the distance $r$ between $A$ and $B$ is $-\frac{dr}{dt} = v_A\cos 0^\circ - v_B\cos(180^\circ - 60^\circ) = v + v\cos 60^\circ = v\left(1 + \frac{1}{2}\right) = \frac{3}{2}v$. Integrating this differential equation from $r = L$ at $t = 0$ to $r = 0$ at $t = T$: $-\int_L^0 dr = \frac{3}{2}v\int_0^T dt \implies L = \frac{3}{2}v T \implies T = \frac{2L}{3v}$. Substituting $L = 60\text{ m}$ and $v = 10\text{ m/s}$, we get $T = \frac{2(60)}{3(10)} = 4\text{ s}$. Since each particle moves with a constant speed $v = 10\text{ m/s}$ along its path, the total distance traversed by each particle is $s = vT = 10 \times 4 = 40\text{ m}$. Therefore, option A is correct.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.questionText: A target particle $P$ moves along the $y$-axis with a constant speed $u = 10\text{ m/s}$ in the positive $y$-direction, starting from the origin at $t = 0$. A pursuer $Q$ starts simultaneously from the point $(d, 0)$ with $d = 120\text{ m}$ on the $x$-axis and moves with a constant speed $v = 20\text{ m/s}$ ($v = 2u$), keeping its velocity vector always pointing directly towards $P$. Find the time $T$ (in seconds) taken by $Q$ to capture $P$.
questions.explanation: Let the instantaneous distance between pursuer $Q$ and target $P$ be $r(t)$, and let $\theta(t)$ be the angle between the line of sight $QP$ and the vertical $y$-axis. The target moves along $+y$ at speed $u$, having a velocity component $u\cos\theta$ away from $Q$ along the line of sight. The pursuer moves directly along the line of sight toward $P$ with speed $v$. Thus, the rate of approach is $-\frac{dr}{dt} = v - u\cos\theta \implies -dr = v\,dt - u\cos\theta\,dt$. Now, the vertical component of the pursuer velocity is $\frac{dy}{dt} = v\cos\theta$, which implies $\cos\theta\,dt = \frac{dy}{v}$. Substituting this yields $-dr = v\,dt - \frac{u}{v}dy$. Integrating this relation from $t = 0$ (where $r = d, y = 0$) to the capture instant $t = T$ (where $r = 0, y = uT$): $-\int_d^0 dr = v\int_0^T dt - \frac{u}{v}\int_0^{uT} dy \implies d = vT - \frac{u^2}{v}T = T\left(\frac{v^2 - u^2}{v}\right)$. Solving for capture time: $T = \frac{vd}{v^2 - u^2}$. Given $v = 20\text{ m/s}$, $u = 10\text{ m/s}$, and $d = 120\text{ m}$, we get $T = \frac{20(120)}{20^2 - 10^2} = \frac{2400}{300} = 8\text{ s}$. Therefore, option A is correct.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.questionText: Two projectiles $A$ and $B$ are fired simultaneously in three-dimensional space under uniform downward gravity $\vec{g} = -10\hat{k}\text{ m/s}^2$. Particle $A$ is launched from the origin $(0, 0, 0)\text{ m}$ with initial velocity $\vec{u}_A = (20\hat{i} + 30\hat{j} + 40\hat{k})\text{ m/s}$. Particle $B$ is launched from position $\vec{r}_{B0} = (80\hat{i} + 40\hat{j} + 0\hat{k})\text{ m}$ with initial velocity $\vec{u}_B = (v_{Bx}\hat{i} + 10\hat{j} + 40\hat{k})\text{ m/s}$. The two particles collide in mid-air at time $t = t_c$. Select the correct statement(s):
options: A) The collision time is $t_c = 2\text{ s}$.
B) The initial velocity component is $v_{Bx} = -20\text{ m/s}$.
C) The vertical height of the collision point above the ground is $z_c = 60\text{ m}$.
D) The magnitude of the relative velocity vector between the two particles is $20\sqrt{5}\text{ m/s}$.
questions.explanation: Both projectiles experience identical gravitational acceleration $\vec{g} = -10\hat{k}\text{ m/s}^2$, so their relative acceleration is identically zero: $\vec{a}_{\text{rel}} = \vec{a}_A - \vec{a}_B = \vec{0}$. Hence, the relative velocity $\vec{v}_{\text{rel}} = \vec{u}_A - \vec{u}_B$ is constant throughout the motion. The position vector of $A$ relative to $B$ is $\vec{r}_{A/B}(t) = (\vec{r}_{A0} - \vec{r}_{B0}) + (\vec{u}_A - \vec{u}_B)t = (-80\hat{i} - 40\hat{j}) + \left[(20 - v_{Bx})\hat{i} + 20\hat{j}\right]t$. For collision to occur at $t = t_c$, $\vec{r}_{A/B}(t_c) = \vec{0}$. Equating the $y$-component: $-40 + 20t_c = 0 \implies t_c = 2\text{ s}$, confirming statement A. Equating the $x$-component: $-80 + (20 - v_{Bx})(2) = 0 \implies 20 - v_{Bx} = 40 \implies v_{Bx} = -20\text{ m/s}$, confirming statement B. The collision position is obtained from particle $A$: $z_c = u_{Az}t_c - \frac{1}{2}gt_c^2 = 40(2) - 5(2)^2 = 80 - 20 = 60\text{ m}$, confirming statement C. The relative velocity vector is $\vec{v}_{\text{rel}} = (20 - (-20))\hat{i} + 20\hat{j} = 40\hat{i} + 20\hat{j}\text{ m/s}$, which has magnitude $|\vec{v}_{\text{rel}}| = \sqrt{40^2 + 20^2} = \sqrt{2000} = 20\sqrt{5}\text{ m/s}$, confirming statement D. Thus, statements A, B, C, and D are all correct.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.questionText: A uniform rigid rod of length $L = 5\text{ m}$ slides with its upper end $A$ on a vertical wall and its lower end $B$ on a horizontal floor. At the instant when the rod makes an angle $\theta = 37^\circ$ with the horizontal floor, end $B$ moves away from the wall with a constant horizontal speed $v_B = 3\text{ m/s}$. Find the magnitude of the acceleration of end $A$ at this instant. (Take $\sin 37^\circ = 3/5$, $\cos 37^\circ = 4/5$).
questions.explanation: Let the horizontal position of end $B$ be $x_B$ and the vertical position of end $A$ be $y_A$. The kinematic constraint of the rigid rod gives $x_B^2 + y_A^2 = L^2$. Differentiating once with respect to time: $2x_B\dot{x}_B + 2y_A\dot{y}_A = 0 \implies x_B v_B + y_A v_A = 0$. Using $x_B = L\cos 37^\circ = 5(4/5) = 4\text{ m}$ and $y_A = L\sin 37^\circ = 5(3/5) = 3\text{ m}$, we solve for $v_A$: $4(3) + 3v_A = 0 \implies v_A = -4\text{ m/s}$ (directed downward). Differentiating the velocity relation once more with respect to time: $\frac{d}{dt}(x_B v_B + y_A v_A) = \dot{x}_B v_B + x_B \dot{v}_B + \dot{y}_A v_A + y_A \dot{v}_A = 0$. Since end $B$ moves with constant speed, $a_B = \dot{v}_B = 0$. Substituting the values: $v_B^2 + 0 + v_A^2 + y_A a_A = 0 \implies 3^2 + (-4)^2 + 3a_A = 0 \implies 25 + 3a_A = 0$. Thus, $a_A = -\frac{25}{3}\text{ m/s}^2$, and its magnitude is $\frac{25}{3}\text{ m/s}^2$. Therefore, option A is correct.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.questionText: A small ring $A$ slides along a fixed horizontal rod. An inextensible light string attached to the ring passes over a small fixed pulley $P$ located at a vertical height $h = 3\text{ m}$ above the rod, and connects to a suspended mass $B$. At the instant when the string segment $AP$ makes an angle $\theta = 30^\circ$ with the horizontal rod, mass $B$ descends vertically at a constant speed $v_B = 4\text{ m/s}$. Find the speed $v_A$ and the magnitude of acceleration $a_A$ of the ring at this instant.
questions.explanation: Let $x$ be the horizontal distance from the point on the rod directly below the pulley to ring $A$, and let $s$ be the distance from the pulley to ring $A$. From geometry, $s = \sqrt{x^2 + h^2}$ and $\cos\theta = \frac{x}{s}$. Since the string is inextensible, $-\dot{s} = v_B$. Differentiating $s^2 = x^2 + h^2$ gives $s\dot{s} = x\dot{x} \implies \dot{s} = \frac{x}{s}\dot{x} = \cos\theta(-v_A) \implies v_B = v_A\cos\theta$. Thus, $v_A = \frac{v_B}{\cos\theta} = \frac{4}{\cos 30^\circ} = \frac{8}{\sqrt{3}}\text{ m/s}$. To find the acceleration, we differentiate $v_A\cos\theta = v_B$ with respect to time. Since $v_B$ is constant, $\frac{d}{dt}(v_A\cos\theta) = 0 \implies a_A\cos\theta - v_A\sin\theta\frac{d\theta}{dt} = 0$. Since $\tan\theta = \frac{h}{x}$, differentiating yields $\sec^2\theta\frac{d\theta}{dt} = -\frac{h}{x^2}\dot{x} = \frac{h v_A}{x^2}$. Using $x = h\cot\theta$, we find $\frac{d\theta}{dt} = \frac{v_A\sin^2\theta}{h}$. Substituting this gives $a_A = \frac{v_A^2\tan\theta\sin^2\theta}{h} = \frac{v_B^2\tan^3\theta}{h}$. For $\theta = 30^\circ$, $\tan 30^\circ = 1/\sqrt{3}$, so $a_A = \frac{4^2 (1/\sqrt{3})^3}{3} = \frac{16}{3 \times 3\sqrt{3}} = \frac{16}{9\sqrt{3}}\text{ m/s}^2$. Therefore, option A is correct.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.questionText: A triangular wedge of inclination angle $\alpha = 60^\circ$ is placed on a smooth horizontal floor. A small block rests on the inclined face of the wedge. The wedge is made to accelerate horizontally to the right with a constant acceleration $a_w = 8\text{ m/s}^2$. If the block slides down along the inclined face with an acceleration $a_r = 5\text{ m/s}^2$ relative to the wedge, find the magnitude of the absolute acceleration of the block with respect to the ground, in m/s$^2$.
questions.explanation: Define the standard Cartesian coordinate system where $\hat{i}$ points horizontally to the right and $\hat{j}$ points vertically upward. The acceleration of the wedge with respect to the ground is $\vec{a}_w = 8\hat{i}\text{ m/s}^2$. The block moves down the inclined surface, which slopes downwards towards the left. The unit vector along the incline downwards is $\hat{u}_{\text{incline}} = -\cos 60^\circ\hat{i} - \sin 60^\circ\hat{j} = -\frac{1}{2}\hat{i} - \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\hat{j}$. The relative acceleration of the block with respect to the wedge is $\vec{a}_r = a_r\hat{u}_{\text{incline}} = 5\left(-\frac{1}{2}\hat{i} - \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\hat{j}\right) = -2.5\hat{i} - 2.5\sqrt{3}\hat{j}\text{ m/s}^2$. The absolute acceleration of the block with respect to the ground is given by the vector sum: $\vec{a}_B = \vec{a}_w + \vec{a}_r = (8 - 2.5)\hat{i} - 2.5\sqrt{3}\hat{j} = 5.5\hat{i} - 2.5\sqrt{3}\hat{j}\text{ m/s}^2$. Computing the magnitude squared: $|\vec{a}_B|^2 = (5.5)^2 + (-2.5\sqrt{3})^2 = 30.25 + 6.25(3) = 30.25 + 18.75 = 49\text{ m}^2/\text{s}^4$. Taking the square root yields $|\vec{a}_B| = \sqrt{49} = 7\text{ m/s}^2$. Hence, the magnitude of the absolute acceleration is $7$ m/s$^2$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.questionText: An anti-aircraft artillery gun on flat ground can fire shells in any direction with a fixed muzzle speed $u = 200\text{ m/s}$. An enemy aircraft flies horizontally at a constant altitude $H = 1500\text{ m}$. Taking $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$, find the maximum horizontal distance $x_{\max}$ from the gun at which the aircraft can be targeted and hit.
questions.explanation: The envelope bounding all possible parabolic trajectories fired with muzzle speed $u$ (known as the parabola of safety) is given by $y = \frac{u^2}{2g} - \frac{g x^2}{2u^2}$. A shell can hit a target at coordinate $(x, y)$ if and only if that point lies within or on this boundary envelope. Setting the target altitude $y = H = 1500\text{ m}$: $1500 = \frac{u^2}{2g} - \frac{g x^2}{2u^2}$. Substituting the values $u = 200\text{ m/s}$ and $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$: $\frac{u^2}{2g} = \frac{200^2}{2(10)} = \frac{40000}{20} = 2000\text{ m}$, and $\frac{g}{2u^2} = \frac{10}{2(40000)} = \frac{1}{8000}\text{ m}^{-1}$. Substituting these numbers into the envelope equation: $1500 = 2000 - \frac{x^2}{8000} \implies \frac{x^2}{8000} = 500 \implies x^2 = 500 \times 8000 = 4\times 10^6\text{ m}^2$. Taking the positive square root gives $x_{\max} = \sqrt{4\times 10^6} = 2000\text{ m}$. Therefore, option A is correct.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.questionText: A particle moves in the $xy$-plane such that its position in polar coordinates $(r, \theta)$ varies with time as $r(t) = r_0 e^{\omega t}$ and $\theta(t) = \omega t$, where $r_0$ and $\omega$ are positive constants. Select the correct statement(s) regarding this motion:
options: A) The velocity vector makes a constant angle of $45^\circ$ with the radial position vector $\vec{r}$ at all times.
B) The radial component of acceleration $a_r$ is identically zero.
C) The magnitude of the total acceleration of the particle is $2\omega^2 r$.
D) The instantaneous speed of the particle is $\sqrt{2}\omega r$.
questions.explanation: In polar coordinates, the velocity components are given by $v_r = \dot{r} = \frac{d}{dt}(r_0 e^{\omega t}) = \omega r_0 e^{\omega t} = \omega r$, and $v_\theta = r\dot{\theta} = r\omega = \omega r$. The angle $\phi$ between the velocity vector and the radial unit vector satisfies $\tan\phi = \frac{v_\theta}{v_r} = \frac{\omega r}{\omega r} = 1 \implies \phi = 45^\circ$, confirming statement A. The speed is $v = \sqrt{v_r^2 + v_\theta^2} = \sqrt{(\omega r)^2 + (\omega r)^2} = \sqrt{2}\omega r$, confirming statement D. For acceleration, the radial component is $a_r = \ddot{r} - r\dot{\theta}^2$. Since $\dot{r} = \omega r$, we have $\ddot{r} = \omega \dot{r} = \omega^2 r$. Thus $a_r = \omega^2 r - r\omega^2 = 0$, confirming statement B. The transverse acceleration is $a_\theta = r\ddot{\theta} + 2\dot{r}\dot{\theta} = r(0) + 2(\omega r)(\omega) = 2\omega^2 r$. The magnitude of total acceleration is $a = \sqrt{a_r^2 + a_\theta^2} = \sqrt{0 + (2\omega^2 r)^2} = 2\omega^2 r$, confirming statement C. Therefore, statements A, B, C, and D are all correct.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.questionText: A flatcar travels along a horizontal straight track with a uniform acceleration $a_c = 2.5\text{ m/s}^2$ directed along the $+x$-direction. A projectile is launched from the platform of the flatcar with a speed $u = 25\text{ m/s}$ relative to the flatcar. Taking $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$, find the launch angle $\theta$ (measured relative to the floor of the flatcar towards $+x$) that maximizes the horizontal range of the projectile relative to the flatcar before it lands back on the platform.
questions.explanation: In the non-inertial reference frame of the flatcar, an inertial pseudo-acceleration $\vec{a}_{\text{pseudo}} = -a_c\hat{i} = -2.5\hat{i}\text{ m/s}^2$ acts horizontally in addition to gravity $\vec{g} = -10\hat{j}\text{ m/s}^2$. The equations of motion in the flatcar frame are $x'(t) = u\cos\theta\,t - \frac{1}{2}a_c t^2$ and $y'(t) = u\sin\theta\,t - \frac{1}{2}g t^2$. The time of flight until the projectile lands back on the flatcar ($y'=0$) is $T = \frac{2u\sin\theta}{g}$. Substituting $T$ into $x'$ gives the range: $R(\theta) = u\cos\theta\left(\frac{2u\sin\theta}{g}\right) - \frac{1}{2}a_c\left(\frac{2u\sin\theta}{g}\right)^2 = \frac{u^2}{g}\left[\sin 2\theta - \frac{2a_c}{g}\sin^2\theta\right]$. Using the trigonometric identity $2\sin^2\theta = 1 - \cos 2\theta$, this becomes $R(\theta) = \frac{u^2}{g}\left[\sin 2\theta + \frac{a_c}{g}\cos 2\theta - \frac{a_c}{g}\right]$. To maximize $R(\theta)$, we differentiate with respect to $\theta$: $\frac{d}{d\theta}\left(\sin 2\theta + \frac{a_c}{g}\cos 2\theta\right) = 2\cos 2\theta - 2\frac{a_c}{g}\sin 2\theta = 0 \implies \tan 2\theta = \frac{g}{a_c}$. Substituting $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$ and $a_c = 2.5\text{ m/s}^2$, we find $\tan 2\theta = \frac{10}{2.5} = 4 \implies \theta = \frac{1}{2}\tan^{-1}(4)$. Therefore, option A is correct.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.questionText: A solid cylinder of radius $R = 0.2\text{ m}$ is placed between two horizontal parallel plates that are moved horizontally in opposite directions. The upper plate moves to the right with a constant speed $v_1 = 6\text{ m/s}$ and the lower plate moves to the left with a constant speed $v_2 = 2\text{ m/s}$. The cylinder rolls without slipping on both plates. Select the correct statement(s):
options: A) The velocity of the center of mass of the cylinder is $2\text{ m/s}$ to the right.
B) The angular velocity of the cylinder is $20\text{ rad/s}$ clockwise.
C) The instantaneous center of zero velocity (ICR) lies at a distance of $0.1\text{ m}$ below the center of mass.
D) The speed of the bottom-most point of the cylinder is $2\text{ m/s}$.
questions.explanation: Let the velocity of the center of mass be $v_{\text{cm}}\hat{i}$ and the clockwise angular velocity be $\omega$. For pure rolling at the contact surfaces: At the top plate, the velocity of the topmost point is $\vec{v}_{\text{top}} = (v_{\text{cm}} + \omega R)\hat{i} = 6\hat{i}\text{ m/s}$, giving $v_{\text{cm}} + \omega R = 6$. At the bottom plate, the velocity of the bottom-most point is $\vec{v}_{\text{bot}} = (v_{\text{cm}} - \omega R)\hat{i} = -2\hat{i}\text{ m/s}$, giving $v_{\text{cm}} - \omega R = -2$. Adding these two equations yields $2v_{\text{cm}} = 4 \implies v_{\text{cm}} = 2\text{ m/s}$ to the right, confirming statement A. Subtracting the two equations yields $2\omega R = 8 \implies \omega R = 4\text{ m/s} \implies \omega = \frac{4}{0.2} = 20\text{ rad/s}$, confirming statement B. The velocity of a point at vertical distance $y$ above the center is $v(y) = v_{\text{cm}} + \omega y$. Setting $v(y) = 0$ gives $y_{\text{ICR}} = -\frac{v_{\text{cm}}}{\omega} = -\frac{2}{20} = -0.1\text{ m}$, meaning the ICR is $0.1\text{ m}$ below the center of mass, confirming statement C. The speed of the bottom point is $|-2\text{ m/s}| = 2\text{ m/s}$, matching the bottom plate, confirming statement D. Thus, statements A, B, C, and D are all correct.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.questionText: A particle executes a three-dimensional helical motion such that its position vector is $\vec{r}(t) = R\cos(\omega t)\hat{i} + R\sin(\omega t)\hat{j} + v_z t\hat{k}$, where $R = 9\text{ m}$, $\omega = 1\text{ rad/s}$, and $v_z = 12\text{ m/s}$. Find the radius of curvature $\rho$ (in metres) of the helical trajectory.
questions.explanation: Differentiating the position vector with respect to time gives the velocity vector: $\vec{v}(t) = \dot{\vec{r}}(t) = -R\omega\sin(\omega t)\hat{i} + R\omega\cos(\omega t)\hat{j} + v_z\hat{k}$. The speed is constant along the trajectory: $v = |\vec{v}| = \sqrt{(-R\omega\sin(\omega t))^2 + (R\omega\cos(\omega t))^2 + v_z^2} = \sqrt{R^2\omega^2 + v_z^2}$. Substituting $R = 9\text{ m}$, $\omega = 1\text{ rad/s}$, and $v_z = 12\text{ m/s}$, we get $R\omega = 9\text{ m/s}$ and $v = \sqrt{9^2 + 12^2} = \sqrt{81 + 144} = \sqrt{225} = 15\text{ m/s}$. Differentiating velocity with respect to time gives the acceleration: $\vec{a}(t) = \ddot{\vec{r}}(t) = -R\omega^2\cos(\omega t)\hat{i} - R\omega^2\sin(\omega t)\hat{j} + 0\hat{k}$. Notice that the dot product is $\vec{v}\cdot\vec{a} = R^2\omega^3\sin(\omega t)\cos(\omega t) - R^2\omega^3\sin(\omega t)\cos(\omega t) + 0 = 0$. Since acceleration is strictly orthogonal to velocity, the tangential acceleration is zero and the normal acceleration is the full acceleration: $a_n = |\vec{a}| = R\omega^2\sqrt{\cos^2(\omega t) + \sin^2(\omega t)} = R\omega^2 = 9(1^2) = 9\text{ m/s}^2$. The radius of curvature is $\rho = \frac{v^2}{a_n} = \frac{15^2}{9} = \frac{225}{9} = 25\text{ m}$. Hence, the radius of curvature is $25$ metres.
